items.title: Two digits by two digits
items.prose: No calculator.
items.question: What is $58 \times 64$?

feedback.generic: Both numbers are 3 from 61. Use a difference of squares.

byKey.no-square: You found $61^2 = 3721$ but did not take off $3^2 = 9$.
byKey.carry: You dropped a hundred. Check with $58 \times 64 = 3480 + 232 = 3712$.
byKey.half: You took off 19 rather than 9. The correction is $3^2$.

explain.text: The mean of 58 and 64 is 61, and each is 3 away. So the product is $61^2 - 3^2 = 3721 - 9 = 3712$. A check: $60 \times 64 - 2 \times 64 = 3840 - 128 = 3712$.

items.title: Sixes count nothing
items.prose: A contract pays the total of three dice in £, but every 6 counts as 0.
items.question: What is the fair value, in £?

feedback.correct: Each die is worth $\tfrac{0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5}{6} = 2.5$, so three are worth £7.50.
feedback.generic: Find the value of one die, then use linearity.

byKey.ignored: You priced the usual total, 10.5. A 6 now pays nothing.
byKey.five-faces: You averaged 1 to 5 over five faces, 3 each. A 6 is still a face: average over all six.
byKey.once: You took 6 off the usual 10.5 once. Each die loses $\tfrac66 = 1$ on average, so take off 3.

explain.text: One die pays $\tfrac{15}{6} = 2.5$ on average. Expectation adds, so three dice are worth $3 \times 2.5 = 7.5$. That is the usual 10.5 less 1 a die.

items.title: Hands at 8:24
items.prose: An analogue clock shows 8:24.
items.question: What is the smaller angle between the hands, in degrees?

feedback.correct: The hour hand is at 252° and the minute hand at 144°: 108° apart.
feedback.generic: The hour hand moves 0.5° a minute, the minute hand 6°.

byKey.fixed-hour: You left the hour hand on the 8. In 24 minutes it moves on by 12°.
byKey.reflex: You gave the larger angle. The smaller one is $360 - 252 = 108$.
byKey.fast-hour: You moved the hour hand 1° a minute. It turns 30° an hour, so 0.5° a minute.

explain.text: The hour hand is at $8 \times 30 + 24 \times 0.5 = 252°$. The minute hand is at $24 \times 6 = 144°$. The gap is $252 - 144 = 108°$.

items.title: Three moves in a row
items.prose: A share falls 20%, then rises 15%, then falls 5%.
items.question: What is its overall change, in per cent? Give one decimal place.

feedback.correct: The factors multiply: $0.8 \times 1.15 \times 0.95 = 0.874$, a fall of 12.6%.
feedback.generic: Turn each move into a factor and multiply.

byKey.added: You added the percentages. Each move acts on the new price, so the factors multiply.
byKey.two-moves: You stopped after two moves, $0.8 \times 1.15 = 0.92$. The last fall of 5% acts on that.
byKey.sign: You found 12.6 but dropped the minus sign. The share ends below where it started.

explain.text: The factors are 0.8, 1.15 and 0.95. First $0.8 \times 1.15 = 0.92$, then $0.92 \times 0.95 = 0.874$. So the share is down 12.6%.

items.title: Edge on a trade
items.prose: Fair value is £50.80. You quote £49.50 at £52.50, and the interviewer buys 3 lots from you.
items.question: What edge, in £, did you make against fair value?

feedback.correct: You sold 3 at £52.50 against a fair £50.80: $3 \times 1.70 = \text{£}5.10$.
feedback.generic: A buyer lifts your ask. Compare the ask with fair value, lot by lot.

byKey.mid: You measured from the middle of your quote, £51. Edge is measured from fair value, £50.80.
byKey.one-lot: You found the edge on one lot. The interviewer bought 3.
byKey.spread: You counted the whole spread on each lot. Only one side traded.
byKey.bid: You used your bid. A buyer trades at your ask, £52.50.

explain.text: The interviewer bought, so you sold at your ask, £52.50. Each lot is £1.70 above fair, and 3 lots make £5.10. The spread pays only when both sides trade.

items.title: A fake among 200
items.prose: One of 200 coins is a fake, heavier than the rest. You have a balance with two pans.
items.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds the fake?

feedback.correct: Each weighing has three outcomes, and $3^4 = 81 < 200 \le 243 = 3^5$, so 5.
feedback.generic: A weighing tells left heavy, right heavy or level. How many coins can $k$ weighings handle?

byKey.halving: You halved the pile each time. Leave a third aside: a level balance says the fake is there.
byKey.log-two: You took $\log_2 200 \approx 7.6$ and rounded down. A balance splits three ways, not two.
byKey.four: Four weighings handle only $3^4 = 81$ coins. 200 needs a fifth.

explain.text: Split the coins into three groups and weigh two of them. Each weighing cuts the suspects to a third, so $k$ weighings handle $3^k$ coins. Since $81 < 200 \le 243$, five weighings are needed and enough.

items.title: Every even face
items.prose: Roll a fair die again and again. Stop once each of 2, 4 and 6 has shown at least once.
items.question: How many rolls do you expect to make?

feedback.correct: The three waits are 2, 3 and 6 rolls, so 11 in all.
feedback.generic: Split the run into waits: for the first even face, then a new one, then the last.

byKey.all-six: You collected all six faces. Only the three even faces are needed, so the odd faces never end a wait.
byKey.three-faces: You treated the die as having three faces. Each roll shows a needed face with chance 3/6, not 3/3.
byKey.six-each: You waited 6 rolls for each face. While two or three faces are still missing, a useful roll is more likely.

explain.text: With $k$ even faces still missing, a roll helps with chance $k/6$, so the wait averages $6/k$. The total is $\tfrac63 + \tfrac62 + \tfrac61 = 2 + 3 + 6 = 11$. The last face costs the most.

items.title: To guess or not
items.prose: A test gives five options for each question. A right answer scores +1, a wrong one −0.25 and a blank 0. You can rule out one option but have no idea among the other four.
items.question: What is the expected mark from guessing? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: Guessing among four is worth $\tfrac14 - \tfrac34 \times 0.25 = 0.0625$ a question.
feedback.generic: Weigh +1 by the chance of a right guess and −0.25 by the chance of a wrong one.

byKey.blind: You guessed among all five. That is worth exactly 0, but ruling one out tips it above 0.
byKey.no-penalty: You forgot the penalty. A wrong guess costs 0.25 with chance $\tfrac34$.
byKey.full-penalty: You charged the penalty as certain. It applies only to the wrong guesses.

explain.text: A guess among four is right with chance $\tfrac14$, so $E = \tfrac14 \times 1 - \tfrac34 \times 0.25 = 0.25 - 0.1875 = 0.0625$. A blind guess from five scores exactly 0. Each option ruled out makes guessing pay.

items.title: Find the equilibrium
items.prose: Row picks Up, Middle or Down. Column picks Left, Centre or Right. Each cell shows (Row's payoff, Column's payoff).
items.question: Tap the cell that is a pure Nash equilibrium.

feedback.correct: At (Middle, Centre) neither player gains by moving alone.
feedback.generic: For each cell, ask: can Row do better in that column, or Column in that row?

byKey.total: You picked the largest total, 7. Row would switch from Up to Middle there, for 3 instead of 2.
byKey.row-best: You picked Row's best payoff, 5. Column would switch from Left to Centre there, for 4 instead of 1.
byKey.both-high: You picked a cell where both do well. Row would switch to Down for 5, and Column to Right for 5.

explain.text: Column's best reply to Middle is Centre, 3 against 0 and 2. Row's best reply to Centre is Middle, 3 against 1 and 0. No other cell is a best reply both ways.

items.title: Stones in a jar
items.prose: A jar holds 9 white and 8 black stones. Take out any two. If they match, put a black stone in. If they differ, put a white stone in. Repeat until one stone is left.
items.question: What colour is the last stone?

options.why: You saw that black is added more often. Count the whites: their number changes by 0 or 2, so it stays odd.

options.text: It depends on the order of the draws
options.why: You tried a few orders without finding what stays fixed. The parity of the whites never changes.

feedback.correct: The number of white stones stays odd, so the last stone is white.
feedback.generic: Track the number of white stones under each kind of move.

explain.text: Two whites out and a black in lowers the whites by 2. Two blacks, or one of each, leaves the whites unchanged. Nine is odd, so the whites stay odd, and a lone stone with an odd white count is white.

items.title: One card turned
items.prose: Ten cards are numbered 1 to 10. Three are dealt face down, and a contract pays their total. The first card is turned over: a 9.
items.question: What is the new fair value? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: The two unseen cards average $\tfrac{46}{9}$ each, so fair is $9 + \tfrac{92}{9} \approx 19.22$.
feedback.generic: Add the known card to two unseen cards, each with the mean of what is left.

byKey.replaced: You gave each unseen card the full mean, 5.5. The 9 has left the deck, so the rest average $\tfrac{46}{9}$.
byKey.one-left: You added one unseen card. Two cards are still face down.
byKey.unchanged: You kept the opening fair, $3 \times 5.5$. The 9 is above the average card, so fair rises.

explain.text: Before the turn, fair was $3 \times 5.5 = 16.5$. The other nine cards total $55 - 9 = 46$, a mean of $\tfrac{46}{9}$. So fair is $9 + 2 \times \tfrac{46}{9} \approx 19.22$.

items.title: Three coins in a bag
items.prose: A bag holds three coins: a fair one, a two-headed one and one that lands heads with chance $\tfrac34$. You draw one at random and toss it twice. Both tosses are heads.
items.question: What is the chance you hold the two-headed coin? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: The chance is $\tfrac{16}{29} \approx 0.5517$.
feedback.generic: Weigh each coin by its chance of two heads, then take the two-headed coin's share.

byKey.prior: You kept the chance before the tosses, $\tfrac13$. Two heads are more likely with the two-headed coin, so its share grows.
byKey.one-toss: You used the chance of one head for each coin. Both tosses count, so square each chance.
byKey.ratio: You left out the fair coin. It explains two heads with chance $\tfrac14$, so it takes a share too.

explain.text: The chances of two heads are $\tfrac14$, $1$ and $\tfrac9{16}$, which add to $\tfrac{29}{16}$. The two-headed coin holds $\tfrac{16}{16}$ of that, so its share is $\tfrac{16}{29} \approx 0.5517$. Equal priors cancel.

items.title: Next in the sequence
items.question: What is the next term?

feedback.correct: The gaps are $1^2, 2^2, 3^2, 4^2$, so the next gap is $5^2 = 25$ and the term is 56.
feedback.generic: Write out the differences between neighbouring terms.

byKey.double: You used "double and add one", which fits 15 to 31 only. The gaps 1, 4, 9, 16 are squares.
byKey.repeat-gap: You repeated the last gap, 16. The gaps grow as squares.
byKey.cube-gap: You added 27, a cube. The gaps are squares, so the next one is 25.

explain.text: The differences are 1, 4, 9 and 16, the squares. The next difference is 25, so the term is $31 + 25 = 56$. Each term is 1 plus a sum of squares.

items.title: How often to play Top
items.prose: A zero-sum game: the table shows what Column pays Row. Row picks Top or Bottom, and Column picks Left or Right.
items.question: In equilibrium, what share of the time does Row play Top? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: Row plays Top $\tfrac37 \approx 0.4286$ of the time, which makes Column indifferent.
feedback.generic: Choose Row's share $p$ so that Left and Right cost Column the same.

byKey.column: You found Column's share on Left, $\tfrac27$. Row's share comes from Column's payoffs being equal.
byKey.value: You found the value of the game, $\tfrac17$. The question asks for Row's share on Top.
byKey.half: You mixed evenly. Then Column plays Right and holds Row to $\tfrac12(-1) + \tfrac12(1) = 0$, below the value.

explain.text: Against Left, Row earns $3p - 2(1 - p) = 5p - 2$. Against Right, $-p + (1 - p) = 1 - 2p$. Setting them equal gives $7p = 3$, so $p = \tfrac37$ and the value is $\tfrac17$.

items.title: A walk on a cube
items.prose: A bug sits on one corner of a cube. Each minute it walks along a random edge to one of the three neighbouring corners.
items.question: How many minutes do you expect it to take to reach the opposite corner?

feedback.correct: Group the corners by distance and the three first-step equations give 10.
feedback.generic: Let $E_k$ be the expected time from a corner $k$ edges from the target. Write one equation for each $k$.

byKey.shortest: You gave the shortest route, 3 edges. The bug walks at random and often steps back.
byKey.adjacent: You found $E_1 = 7$, the time from a corner next to the target. The bug starts three edges away.
byKey.two-away: You found $E_2 = 9$, the time from two edges away. The start is three edges away, one step further.

explain.text: From three edges away every step goes to distance 2: $E_3 = 1 + E_2$. Then $E_2 = 1 + \tfrac13 E_3 + \tfrac23 E_1$ and $E_1 = 1 + \tfrac23 E_2$. Solving gives $E_1 = 7$, $E_2 = 9$ and $E_3 = 10$.

items.title: After being lifted
items.prose: Fair value is £48.50 and you quote £47.50 at £49.50. The interviewer buys 3 lots from you, and nothing changes fair value. Your rule: half-width £1, and move the centre £0.50 for each lot held.
items.question: What is your next quote?

options.why: You moved the centre down. You are short 3, so you want buyers to stop: move up to attract sellers.
You left the quote alone. Fair has not moved, but your position has, and the rule skews for it.
You skewed for one lot. The interviewer bought 3 lots, so move $3 \times \text{£}0.50$.

feedback.correct: Short 3, you lift the centre by £1.50 to £50, so you quote £49 at £51.
feedback.generic: Work out your position, then the centre: fair plus £0.50 for each lot short.

explain.text: Selling 3 leaves you short 3. A short position wants sellers, so the centre moves up: $48.50 + 3 \times 0.50 = 50$. With half-width £1 the quote is £49 at £51.

items.title: The last counter loses
items.prose: There are 38 counters. Two players take turns removing 1, 2, 3 or 4. Whoever takes the last counter loses. You move first.
items.question: How many counters should you take?

feedback.correct: Leave 36, one more than a multiple of 5: take 2.
feedback.generic: Work back from the end. Which piles lose for the player about to move?

byKey.normal-play: You left 35, a multiple of 5. That wins when the last counter wins. Here it loses, so leave one more than a multiple of 5.
byKey.one: You left 37. Your rival takes 1 and leaves you 36, a losing pile.
byKey.most: You took the most you could and left 34. Your rival then leaves 31, and you lose.

explain.text: A pile of 1 loses for the mover, and so do 6, 11, 16 and so on. Whatever you take, the rival makes the round total 5. From 38, take 2 to leave 36.

items.title: Odds of 3 to 2
items.prose: A bet pays 3 to 2: each £1 staked wins £1.50 or is lost. It wins with chance $\tfrac12$.
items.question: What fraction of your bankroll does the Kelly rule stake? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: Kelly stakes $f^* = \tfrac12 - \tfrac{1/2}{3/2} = \tfrac16 \approx 0.1667$.
feedback.generic: Use $f^* = p - q/b$ with $b$ the net odds.

byKey.edge: You staked the edge, £0.25 a pound. Kelly divides the edge by the odds: $0.25 / 1.5 = \tfrac16$.
byKey.p: You staked the chance of winning. That fraction risks too much: one loss halves the bankroll.
byKey.evens: You treated the bet as evens, where a fair coin has no edge. At 3 to 2 a win pays more than a loss costs.

explain.text: Here $b = 1.5$, $p = q = \tfrac12$. So $f^* = p - \tfrac{q}{b} = \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac16$. It is the edge per pound, 0.25, divided by the odds, 1.5.

items.title: A square root by hand
items.prose: No calculator.
items.question: Estimate $\sqrt{1900}$ to two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Start from the nearest square below, $43^2 = 1849$, and correct by the leftover over twice the root.

byKey.no-halve: You divided the leftover 51 by 43. The correction is $51/(2 \times 43)$, because $(43 + d)^2 \approx 1849 + 86d$.
byKey.square: You rounded up to 44. But $44^2 = 1936$, which overshoots 1900 by 36.
byKey.fifty: You took the midpoint of 43 and 44. But $43.5^2 = 1892.25$, still short of 1900, so the root is higher.

explain.text: Write $\sqrt{1900} = 43 + d$. Then $1849 + 86d \approx 1900$, so $d \approx 51/86 \approx 0.593$. The true value is 43.589, and the tiny overshoot is the $d^2$ we dropped.

items.title: Six estimates of a jar
items.prose: Six bidders each estimate the value of a jar. Each error is uniform from −£12 to +£12, independent of the others. Everyone bids their estimate, and the highest wins.
items.question: On average, by how much does the winning estimate exceed the value, in £? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: The largest of six errors averages $12 \times \tfrac57 \approx \text{£}8.57$.
feedback.generic: The winner holds the largest error. Write each error as $-12 + 24U$.

byKey.zero: You used the average error, 0. The winner is the bidder with the largest error, which is biased up.
byKey.largest: You took the largest possible error. Six draws rarely reach the top of the range.
byKey.no-shift: You took $\tfrac67$ of 12. The largest $U$ averages $\tfrac67$, so the error averages $-12 + 24 \times \tfrac67$.

explain.text: The largest of six uniforms on 0 to 1 averages $\tfrac67$. So the winning error averages $-12 + 24 \times \tfrac67 = 12 \times \tfrac57 \approx 8.57$. A bidder should shade by that much to break even when winning.

items.title: A die against a coin
items.prose: Ana and Ben take turns, Ana first. On her turn Ana rolls a die and wins on a 5 or a 6. On his turn Ben tosses a coin and wins on heads.
items.question: What is the chance Ana wins? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: Ana wins with chance exactly $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Let $x$ be Ana's chance at the start of a round. Write $x$ in terms of itself.

byKey.ratio: You split by the chances alone, $\tfrac{1/3}{1/3 + 1/2}$. Ana moves first, and that is worth something.
byKey.one-turn: You gave Ana's chance on her first turn only. If both miss, the game starts again.
byKey.flipped: You found Ben's share by the ratio and gave it to Ana. Write the round equation instead.

explain.text: Ana wins at once with chance $\tfrac13$, or both miss with chance $\tfrac23 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac13$ and the game restarts. So $x = \tfrac13 + \tfrac13 x$, which gives $x = \tfrac12$. Moving first exactly offsets her worse odds each turn.

items.title: Next in line
items.prose: The numbers 1 to 10 are shuffled into a random row. Count the $k$ from 1 to 9 for which $k + 1$ sits directly to the right of $k$.
items.question: What is the expected count? Give one decimal place.

feedback.correct: Each of the 9 pairs has chance $\tfrac1{10}$, so the count averages 0.9.
feedback.generic: Use one indicator for each $k$ and find its chance by symmetry.

byKey.either-way: You counted $k + 1$ on either side of $k$. The question asks for $k + 1$ directly to the right only.
byKey.one: You recalled the hats answer, 1. Here there are 9 pairs, each with chance $\tfrac1{10}$.
byKey.squared: You squared the chance $\tfrac1{10}$. Gluing $k$ and $k + 1$ into one block already gives the pair's chance, $9!/10! = \tfrac1{10}$.

explain.text: Glue $k$ and $k + 1$ into one block: $9!$ of the $10!$ rows contain it, a chance of $\tfrac1{10}$. Linearity adds the 9 indicators, so $E = \tfrac9{10} = 0.9$. The indicators are dependent, but linearity does not need independence.

items.title: Rank five chances
items.prose: No calculator. Rank these events from most likely to least likely.
items.question: Put the events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in four rolls of a die
Two cards from a full deck share a colour
At least three heads in four tosses of a coin
One card from a full deck is an ace or a picture card

feedback.generic: Turn each into a fraction you can compare: $1 - (\tfrac56)^4$, $\tfrac{25}{51}$, $\tfrac5{16}$, $\tfrac4{13}$ and $\tfrac{10}{36}$.

byKey.b: You put the shared colour first. $\tfrac{25}{51}$ is just under a half, but $1 - (\tfrac56)^4 = \tfrac{671}{1296}$ is just over.
byKey.e: You put the ace or picture card above three heads. Cross-multiply: $5 \times 13 = 65$ beats $4 \times 16 = 64$, so $\tfrac5{16}$ is larger.
byKey.d: You ranked the dice total too high. Only 10 of the 36 rolls total 9 or more.
byKey.c: You ranked three heads too high. Only 5 of the 16 outcomes have three or four heads.

explain.text: A six in four rolls has chance $1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} \approx 0.518$, and a shared colour $\tfrac{25}{51} \approx 0.490$. Then $\tfrac5{16} = 0.3125$ just beats $\tfrac4{13} \approx 0.308$, by cross-multiplying. Last is $\tfrac{10}{36} \approx 0.278$.

items.title: A put from a call
items.prose: Contracts settle on $S$, the total of three dice. The 12-call pays $\max(S - 12, 0)$ and is worth $\tfrac7{12} \approx 0.5833$.
items.question: What is the 12-put, paying $\max(12 - S, 0)$, worth? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: By parity, the put is $\tfrac7{12} + (12 - 10.5) = \tfrac{25}{12} \approx 2.0833$.
feedback.generic: A long call and a short put at one strike pay $S - 12$ on every roll.

byKey.sign: You took 1.5 off the call. The strike is above the mean, so the put is the dearer one: $P = C + (12 - 10.5)$.
byKey.same: You priced the put like the call. Three dice are symmetric about 10.5, not 12, so they differ.
byKey.two-dice: You used 7 as the mean total. That is two dice: three dice average 10.5.

explain.text: On every roll the call pays minus the put pays $S - 12$. Take expectations: $C - P = E[S] - 12 = 10.5 - 12 = -1.5$. So $P = 0.5833 + 1.5 = 2.0833$, which a direct count, $\tfrac{450}{216}$, confirms.

items.title: A shrinking bonus pool
items.prose: Ana and Ben split a £100 pool. Ana proposes a split; if Ben refuses, the pool falls to £70 and Ben proposes. Refusals then take it to £40 with Ana proposing, then £10 with Ben. A last refusal leaves both with nothing.
items.question: What does Ana keep in round 1, in £? Assume a player accepts when indifferent.

feedback.correct: Working back gives the proposers 10, 30, 40 and then 60 for Ana.
feedback.generic: Start in the last round. A proposer offers the responder what they would get next round.

byKey.even: You split evenly. The proposer has the power each round, and the threats set the shares.
byKey.last-threat: You offered Ben only his £10 from round 4. If he refuses, he proposes in round 2 and gets more.
byKey.three-rounds: You stopped at £40. The fourth round gives Ben £10 there, which shifts every earlier share.

explain.text: In round 4 Ben keeps £10, so in round 3 Ana gives him 10 and keeps 30. In round 2 Ben gives Ana 30 and keeps 40. So in round 1 Ana gives Ben 40 and keeps £60.

items.title: A fair bit from a biased coin
items.prose: A coin lands heads with chance 0.3. To make a fair bit, toss it in pairs. HT means 1 and TH means 0; after HH or TT, toss another pair.
items.question: How many tosses do you expect to use for one bit? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: Each pair succeeds with chance 0.42, so a bit costs $2 / 0.42 \approx 4.76$ tosses.
feedback.generic: Find the chance that one pair gives a bit, then the expected number of pairs.

byKey.rounds: You counted pairs, $1/0.42 \approx 2.38$. Each pair is two tosses.
byKey.one-pair: You assumed the first pair always gives a bit. HH and TT happen with chance 0.58 here.
byKey.one-order: You kept only HT, with chance 0.21. TH also gives a bit, so a pair works with chance 0.42.

explain.text: HT and TH each have chance $0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.21$, so they are equally likely and the bit is fair. A pair works with chance 0.42, so the number of pairs is geometric with mean $1/0.42 \approx 2.381$. That is $2/0.42 \approx 4.76$ tosses.

items.title: Call or fold on the river
items.prose: The pot is £75, and your rival bets £50. Your hand beats only a bluff. You judge that a third of their bets here are bluffs.
items.question: What is the expected value of calling, in £? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: Calling wins £125 a third of the time and loses £50 otherwise: $\tfrac{125 - 100}{3} \approx \text{£}8.33$.
feedback.generic: If you call and win, you take the pot and their bet. If you lose, you lose your call.

byKey.pot-only: You left their £50 bet out of what you win. A won call takes the pot and the bet, £125.
byKey.no-loss: You counted only the wins. Two thirds of the time you lose the £50 call.
byKey.no-bet: You counted a third of the pot and no losses. Add their bet to the win and take off the lost calls.

explain.text: EV $= \tfrac13 \times 125 - \tfrac23 \times 50 = 41.67 - 33.33 = 8.33$. The pot odds say a call needs $\tfrac{50}{175} \approx 28.6\%$ bluffs. A third is more, so calling pays.

items.title: Two windows
items.prose: Ana arrives at a uniform time from 12:00 to 13:00 and waits 15 minutes. Ben arrives at a uniform time from 12:30 to 13:30 and waits 5 minutes. Their times are independent.
items.question: What is the chance they meet? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: They meet with chance $\tfrac7{36} \approx 0.1944$.
feedback.generic: Measure minutes from 12:00 and write the meeting condition in terms of $B - A$.

byKey.same-window: You gave both people the window 12:00 to 13:00. Ben's window starts half an hour later.
byKey.swapped: You let Ana wait 5 minutes and Ben 15. Ana waits for Ben when she is first, so $B - A$ may reach 15.
byKey.both-15: You let both wait 15 minutes. Ben leaves after 5, so Ana must arrive within 5 minutes of him.

explain.text: With $A$ on 0 to 60 and $B$ on 30 to 90, they meet when $-5 \le B - A \le 15$. Write $B = 30 + Y$: then $Y - A$ lies in $[-35, -15]$, and $Y - A$ has the triangle density $(60 - |z|)/3600$. Its area there is $\int_{15}^{35} (60 - z)\,dz / 3600 = 700/3600 = \tfrac7{36}$.

items.title: A four-dice desk
items.prose: A contract settles at the total of four dice, rolled one at a time. Each turn you quote a bid, an ask and a size. Your limit is 4 lots either way, and your spread must be £1 to £4.
items.question: Play the 8 turns. Finish with a P&L of at least £4 and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: No dice are rolled yet. Four dice average £14.
The first two dice show 6 and 5. Fair is now £18.
The third die shows 4. Fair is now £18.50. From now on a client trades who has seen the last die.

feedback.correct: You moved with each card, kept your size inside the limit and stayed out of the informed client's way.
feedback.generic: Read the results table: look for trades against stale prices and for any turn whose size broke the limit.

items.title: A market on the wait for a six
items.prompt:
An interviewer says: "I will roll a fair die until the first 6. The contract settles at £1 for each roll, the 6 included. Make me a market." Write your answer as you would say it.

1. Give the fair value, with its argument.
2. Give a two-sided quote, and say why it is as wide as it is.
3. The interviewer buys 3 lots at your ask of £7. Then four rolls pass with no 6. Mark your position.
4. Give your new quote, and say how your position shapes it.
items.model:
**1. Fair value.** The number of rolls $N$ is geometric with $p = \tfrac16$, so $E[N] = \tfrac1p = 6$. First-step check: $E = 1 + \tfrac56 E$ gives $E = 6$. Fair is £6.

**2. Quote.** The spread of $N$ is large: $\operatorname{Var}(N) = \tfrac{q}{p^2} = 30$, so the standard deviation is about 5.5. The distribution is skewed: the median is 4, but long waits pull the mean up to 6. I would quote £5 at £7, wide because one contract can settle anywhere from 1 to 20 or more.

**3. Mark.** Rolls have no memory, so after four misses the remaining wait is still worth 6. Fair is now $4 + 6 = \text{£}10$. I sold 3 at £7, so I am short 3 and down $3 \times (10 - 7) = \text{£}9$ on the mark.

**4. New quote.** I centre on the new fair, £10, then skew up for the short position: £0.25 a lot gives £10.75. With a width of £2 I quote £9.75 at £11.75. A higher bid invites sellers, who would cut my short. I would also keep my size small, because the settlement can still be far above £10.

rubric.text: Fair value £6, with a reason: the geometric mean $1/p$ or a first-step equation.
A quote around £6, its width justified by the spread of the wait (sd about 5.5) or its long tail.
Uses memorylessness: after four misses fair is $4 + 6 = \text{£}10$, not £6 and not £2.
Marks the short 3 lots correctly: a loss of $3 \times (10 - 7) = \text{£}9$.
New quote centred near £10 and skewed up for the short position, with a reason (attract sellers, cut risk).
